what_it_does: Content-Addressable Memory (CAM) is a special kind of memory you search by content rather than by address — you hand it a pattern and it tells you where that pattern lives, which is useful in networking, databases, and AI lookup tables. Implementing CAM on FPGAs (reconfigurable chips where you program the logic yourself) traditionally uses a lot of look-up tables or block RAM, the chip's two main logic resources, and runs slowly when you need to search many entries at once. This paper proposes building CAM out of DSP blocks instead — the arithmetic units on FPGAs normally reserved for signal processing and math — because those blocks happen to contain small on-chip memories and logic that can be repurposed for parallel search. The design lets you tune the CAM's width, depth, and how many searches it handles simultaneously, so it can be tailored to specific applications without wasting chip area.
